title: Seeing vs. Doing: Pearl's Do-Calculus, Rubin's Potential Outcomes, and the Causal Revolution on Trial — From Sewall Wright's path diagrams & Neyman's urns to Rubin's 1974 Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) potential outcomes & SUTVA; Pearl's 1995 Biometrika DAGs, collider bias, back-door/front-door criteria & complete symbolic do-calculus; Angrist, Imbens & Rubin's 1996 Nobel LATE complier theorem & Bareinboim-Pearl selection-diagram transportability; Dawid's 2000 Popperian assault on metaphysical cross-world counterfactuals, Aronow & Samii's 2017 network interference refutation of naive SUTVA & Imbens's 2020 DAGs-vs-econometrics critique; Python-verified front-door, defier & collider math

teenKit.tldr: For nearly a century, science was trapped looking at mere passive correlations until a mathematical revolution finally cracked the code to separate what we see from what we actually do. By inventing tools like potential outcomes and causal diagrams, researchers learned how to stop spreadsheets from lying and finally prove true cause and effect.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Mastering the difference between seeing and doing is the ultimate mental superpower for surviving a world flooded with biased data, misleading headlines, and fake medical claims.
keyTakeaways: Correlation is a notorious liar: just because two things happen together doesn't mean one caused the other, which caused a century-long paralysis in statistics.
Donald Rubin's Potential Outcomes framework imagines a parallel universe where we compare what happened to a person versus what would have happened if we did something else.

Judea Pearl's Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and do-calculus give computers and scientists an actual mathematical algebra to map out hidden confounders and predict the exact results of physical actions.

vocab.meaning: A statistical pattern where two things move together, but neither is necessarily causing the other.
The twin possibilities of what would happen to someone under a treatment versus under a control scenario.
A statistical trap where controlling for a common effect of two independent variables accidentally creates a fake, misleading link between them.
A specialized mathematical language created by Judea Pearl to calculate the real-world effects of active physical interventions.

quiz.question: Why did classical statistics banish the word 'cause' for nearly a hundred years?
options: Because computers weren't powerful enough to run spreadsheets.
Because mathematicians lacked a formal algebra to distinguish passive seeing from active doing.
Because ancient philosophers proved cause and effect doesn't exist.
Because everyone agreed correlation was always better than causation.
quiz.explanation: Early statisticians lacked the mathematical language to prove physical interventions, forcing them to rely entirely on passive observation.

quiz.question: What is the core idea behind Donald Rubin's Potential Outcomes framework?
options: Comparing a person's actual outcome under a treatment with the counterfactual outcome if they hadn't received it.
Guessing future stock market prices using a random number generator.
Drawing arrows between variables to see which way the wind blows.
Averaging out all the errors in a hospital database until it looks perfect.
quiz.explanation: Rubin's model focuses on comparing the reality we can measure against the alternate parallel universe where a different choice was made.

quiz.question: What danger does a collider represent in a causal graph?
options: It speeds up how fast data travels through a computer network.
It acts as a shield that blocks all forms of bias automatically.
It is a 'bad control' that, when adjusted for, tricks you into seeing a false relationship between independent things.
It completely destroys the internet server hosting the spreadsheet.
quiz.explanation: Controlling for a collider creates a statistical illusion, opening up a backdoor path that corrupts your analysis with total bias.
